name: Unggumi
confidence_why: No source describes Unggumi stress: McGregor and Rumsey (2009) only mention "initial stressed syllables" in passing while discussing the language's mid vowels, and Capell (1940), Capell and Coate (1984), McGregor (1988), Clendon (2014) and PHOIBLE say nothing about it, so initial stress here is an inference from one aside and the Kimberley norm, not a documented rule.
catalog_citation: McGregor, William B. & Alan Rumsey. 2009. Worrorran revisited: the case for genetic relations among languages of the Northern Kimberley region of Western Australia. (Pacific Linguistics 600.) Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. xi+120 pp. hdl 1885/50063 (ANU Open Research, open access).
catalog_locator: p. 22 (p. 35 of the ANU Open Research file), Chapter 4 'Phonology', section 4.1 'Modern Worrorran phonologies', paragraph beginning 'By contrast, in Unggumi' rendered
catalog_quote: By contrast, in Unggumi, among the several hundred recorded words in the language, there are very few examples of the mid vowels /e/ and /o/ within non-bound morphemes, especially within initial stressed syllables such as those shown above. In this environment there are only ten attested examples, five with e and five with o or o:. Moreover, in some of the words which have mid vowels in other Worrorran languages and apparent cognates in Unggumi, the latter have other vowels or sequences in place of the mid vowels. Thus, for the above words the corresponding forms in Unggumi (with the same meanings) are, respectively: thayigulanya (with feminine noun class suffix -nya), batha, jali and jawingarri.

In this environment there are only ten attested examples, five with e and five with o or o.' Verbatim, locator correct (also lines 1700-1703 of the). The Google Books feed snippet for the volume (wqgpAQAAIAAJ) shows the same sentence. Context read: Ch.4 (pp.20-34) has sections 4.1 phonologies, 4.2 lamino-dental correspondences,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated anywhere. The sentence presupposes that the initial syllable of Unggumi lexical words (the cited examples are disyllables batha, jali and trisyllables jawingarri, thayigulanya) is the stressed syllable, i.e. word-initial stress, consistent with the initial-stress pattern described for the related Worrorran languages Ngarinyin (Capell 1970) and Worrorra (Clendon 2014). This is an incidental presupposition by the two linguists who recorded the last speakers, not a description of the stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Capell & Coate (1984:7) note grammatically contrastive vowel length in one Unggumi verb pair (jawirganimen 'he rubbed himself' vs jawirga:nimen 'they rubbed themselves'); no interaction with stress is described.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical words in a comparative wordlist (citation forms); nothing on phrase-level stress. The remark is made in a discussion of vowel distribution, not of prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Unggumi (ungg1243, ISO xgu, Austlang K14; also Ungumi, Ungami, Wunggumi, Oonggoomi, Wongkomi) is 'consistently regarded as a separate language' within the Worrorric group (McGregor & Rumsey 2009:5). The PL-600 data come from Rumsey's (1984) and McGregor's (1985-87) fieldwork with the last speaker(s) in Derby (consultant Bill (Morndi) Munro named in the acknowledgements) plus Capell's 1938-39 and Coate's material; no dialect distinctions are drawn.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur & H.H.J. Coate. 1984. Comparative studies in Northern Kimberley languages. Pacific Linguistics C-69. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Ch.1 'Preliminary: phonological principles' pp.7-17 (incl. 1.1.3 'The syllable') has no stress/accent section. The 16 incidental stress remarks in the book concern Worora, Ngarinjin and Wunambal (e.g. p.4 'one of the very rare accents on a final syllable'; p.79 'The fixity of the stress is noticeable also, even if it has to fall four syllables back from the end' [Worora kin terms]; p.142 gunjagu 'with stress now on the second syllable' [Ngarinjin]). None of the 82 Unggumi mentions co-occurs with a stress remark. Unggumi phonology notes: interdentals (p.7), grammatical vowel length jawirganime…
